explanations.explanation: Blind is it, friend. Verse 10 says, "Israel’s watchmen are blind, they are all oblivious…" (Isaiah 56:10). A watchman is there to spot trouble early, and these ones aren't seeing any of it. That's why the verse is so serious.

Wounded sounds reasonable, because a hurt guard can't guard well. But the verse never mentions an injury. It says the watchmen are blind, oblivious and loving to slumber. So the trouble is with their seeing, not with a bandage.

Missing would at least explain an empty post. But the watchmen are right there, described as dreamers lying around who love to slumber. They're present and not watching anything. A watchman asleep on the job is almost funnier than one who skipped work.

I get why you'd think so, since watchdogs are supposed to bark. But the verse says the opposite: these watchmen are mute dogs, and they cannot bark. They're also dreamers lying around, loving to slumber. This is a watchdog that's snoring on the porch.
False is right. Verse 10 calls them mute dogs that cannot bark. A dog that can't bark at the burglar is basically a very furry doorstop. The picture is of watchmen who aren't warning anybody.

Discernment, baker. Verse 11 calls them shepherds with no discernment, and says they all turn to their own way. Those two go together in the verse. It's like a baker who can't tell when the cookies are done and just walks off.

Strength is a fair guess, since shepherds do a lot of walking and carrying. But verse 11 doesn't say they lack strength. It says they are shepherds with no discernment, and they all turn to their own way.

Flock makes sense because we're talking about shepherds. But the verse doesn't say the flock is gone. It says the shepherds have no discernment and each one turns to his own way. A shepherd can have a whole flock and still lead it nowhere good.
His own gain, friend. Verse 11 says each one is seeking his own gain. That's a baker who takes the whole cookie box home and tells the guests the oven broke.
The king's approval sounds like something a shepherd could chase. But the verse never brings in a king. It says each one is seeking his own gain. The target is his own pocket, not a throne.

Revenge would make for a dramatic story. But verse 11 doesn't mention rivals or payback. Each shepherd turns to his own way, seeking his own gain. It's less of a feud and more of a me-first free-for-all.

That's it. They say, “…tomorrow will be like today, only far better!” (Isaiah 56:12). It's somebody sitting down with a tray of cookies, saying tomorrow will be just like today, only bigger. They're planning on more of the same, with extra.

That's a gloomy forecast, but it's not what they say. In verse 12 they call for wine and strong drink, and they say tomorrow will be like today, only far better. Their words look ahead to more of the same, and bigger.

Nothing like today would mean they expect a total change. But the verse has them saying tomorrow will be like today, only far better. They want more of the same, and bigger. It's the "same party, louder music" plan.

explanations.answer: They are taken from the presence of evil
explanations.explanation: Right. Verse 1 says no one considers that the righteous are taken away from the presence of evil. I think this one is tender, friend. Verse 2 follows with those who walk uprightly entering into peace.

explanations.answer: They are punished for hidden sins
explanations.explanation: That's a common thought when someone is taken, but the verse doesn't say it. It says the righteous are taken away from the presence of evil. Nothing in it points to hidden sins. I think this is a gentle verse, and it deserves a gentle read.

That's a hopeful guess, but this verse doesn't say they'll come back. What it says is that no one considers that the righteous are taken away from the presence of evil. Then verse 2 says those who walk uprightly enter into peace. I think this part is a tender one.

True. Verse 2 says those who walk uprightly enter into peace, and “they find rest, lying down in death.” It's a quiet verse, and I think a comforting one. Notice the word peace shows up here, and it comes back at the end of the passage.
It's actually true, friend. Verse 2 says those who walk uprightly enter into peace, and “they find rest, lying down in death.” The verse holds rest for the upright. I think it's a gentle one.

True. God asks, “Are you not children of transgression, offspring of deceit…” (Isaiah 57:4). It's a hard question. God asks it right after asking whom they're mocking and sneering at. This is one of the heavier parts of the passage.

It's actually true, baker. In verse 4 God asks, “Are you not children of transgression, offspring of deceit…” It comes right after His questions about who they're mocking and sneering at. This is one of the heavier parts of the passage.

explanations.answer: Whether He should relent because of them
explanations.explanation: Yes. God asks, “Should I relent because of these?” (Isaiah 57:6). He asks it about the drink offering and the grain offering given to the smooth stones. He's asking, not telling, and the question hangs there.

explanations.answer: Who taught them to bring such offerings
explanations.explanation: That's a natural question to wonder about, but it's not what God asks. Verse 6 has Him asking, “Should I relent because of these?” The text never says who taught them anything. I'd stick with what's written.

explanations.answer: When they will come back to Him
explanations.explanation: That would be a welcoming question, but it isn't the one in verse 6. God asks, “Should I relent because of these?” It's about the offerings to the smooth stones.
Forsaking is it. Verse 8 says, “Forsaking Me…” and then goes on to the uncovered bed. It's God Himself saying it. The bed on the hill and the memorial behind the door come with leaving Him.
Obeying doesn't fit, baker. In verse 8 God says, “Forsaking Me…” and the words after it describe the bed and the pact. Nothing in the verse sounds like obedience. It's the opposite direction.
Praising would be a happy ending for this verse, but it's not the one here. God says, “Forsaking Me…” in verse 8. The memorial behind the door and the bed they uncovered go with that.
A great distance, friend. Verse 9 says they sent their envoys, the messengers they sent out, a great distance. That's the long-haul route, not a quick errand. Those envoys earned every mile.

The next town would be a short trip, and the verse says the opposite. God says they sent their envoys a great distance. That's not a ride around the block. The text goes on to say they descended even to Sheol itself.
Across the river sounds like a modest trip. But verse 9 says they sent their envoys a great distance. No river shows up in the verse. The distance is the point.
That's what you'd expect from someone worn out, but verse 10 says the opposite. They did not say, “There is no hope!” Instead they found renewal of their strength. They kept going.
False is right. God says in verse 10 that they did not say, “There is no hope!” They found renewal of their strength, so they didn't grow weak. Tired, yes, but still on the road.
That's the one. God asks, “Is it not because I have long been silent that you do not fear Me?” (Isaiah 57:11). It's a question He puts to them. I'd just let the question stand the way He asked it.
Moved far away isn't in the verse. God asks, “Is it not because I have long been silent that you do not fear Me?” The reason He raises is His silence, not a distance. Those are two different things.

That could explain a lot, but it's not what the verse says. God says they lied and failed to remember Him. The reason He raises is in His question: “Is it not because I have long been silent that you do not fear Me?” (Isaiah 57:11).

Close, but it's the other way around. God says, “I will expose your righteousness and your works, and they will not profit you.” (Isaiah 57:12). Their works won't pay off. That's a sweat-for-nothing situation.

False is right. In verse 12 God says, “I will expose your righteousness and your works, and they will not profit you.” So all that effort doesn't pay them back. It's like stamping a hundred cookies and not one of them going in the box.

Idols, baker. God says, “…let your companies of idols deliver you!” (Isaiah 57:13). A crowd of idols, and not one of them is a rescuer. The crowd looks impressive, and that's about all it has going for it.
Soldiers would be a sensible thing to cry out to. But verse 13 doesn't mention soldiers. God says, “…let your companies of idols deliver you!” It's the idols being put to the test.

Envoys did come up earlier, in verse 9, when they sent them a great distance. But in verse 13 the ones God points to for rescue are the idols. He says, “…let your companies of idols deliver you!” The envoys are a different part of the picture.
True. God says, “…the wind will carry off all of them, a breath will take them away.” (Isaiah 57:13). It's like a receipt blowing across a parking lot. Gone with one gust.
It's actually true, friend. Verse 13 says, “…the wind will carry off all of them, a breath will take them away.” All of them, not just a few. A single breath is enough.

Yes. God says, “…he who seeks refuge in Me will inherit the land and possess My holy mountain.” (Isaiah 57:13). The one who seeks refuge in God gets the inheritance. That's a nice turn after all those idols.

Counting offerings sounds like a fair system, but it's not the one in the verse. God says, “…he who seeks refuge in Me will inherit the land and possess My holy mountain.” It's about seeking refuge in Him. There's no scoreboard.

explanations.answer: Whoever was born in the land
explanations.explanation: Being born there seems like a safe bet, but the verse doesn't say it. God says, “…he who seeks refuge in Me will inherit the land and possess My holy mountain.” What counts is seeking refuge in Him. Birthplace never comes up.

explanations.answer: The oppressed and humble in spirit
explanations.explanation: That's it. The Holy One says, “I dwell in a high and holy place, and with the oppressed and humble in spirit…” (Isaiah 57:15). He's high and holy, and He's also near the humble. I love that both are in the same verse.

explanations.answer: The mighty and wise in heart
explanations.explanation: The mighty and wise would be an impressive crowd. But in verse 15 the Holy One says He dwells with “…the oppressed and humble in spirit…” The verse names a different group than the mighty and wise.

explanations.answer: The priests who serve at His altar
explanations.explanation: Priests are a natural guess, but they don't appear in this verse. God says He dwells with the oppressed and humble in spirit. The verse names people by how low they are, not by their job.
True. Verse 15 says He is there to “…revive the heart of the contrite.” The contrite are the ones who are humble and sorry. A revived heart is a good thing to have after a long stretch of rough days.
It's actually true, friend. In verse 15 the Holy One says He dwells with the humble to “…revive the heart of the contrite.” He's reviving them, not turning them away. It's a warm verse.

explanations.answer: Man's spirit would grow weak before Him
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says, “for then the spirit of man would grow weak before Me—the breath of life I have made.” (Isaiah 57:16). He ties it to the breath of life He made. It's His own reason, and He gives it.

explanations.answer: His people have paid for their sins
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a tidy reason, but it's not the one in the verse. God says, “for then the spirit of man would grow weak before Me—the breath of life I have made.” He doesn't mention a payment here. The reason is about the spirit of man and the breath He made.

explanations.answer: His anger fades with the years
explanations.explanation: Anger fading over time is how it goes with people, but this verse doesn't say it. God gives a different reason: “for then the spirit of man would grow weak before Me—the breath of life I have made.” (Isaiah 57:16). It's about the spirit of man, not a clock.

True. Verse 17 says, “yet he kept turning back to the desires of his heart.” God struck him, and he still kept turning back. This is a heavy verse. It makes what comes next in verse 18 stand out all the more.

It's actually true, baker. Verse 17 says, “yet he kept turning back to the desires of his heart.” Even after being struck, he went right back. That makes what comes next in verse 18 even more striking.
Heal, friend. God says, “I have seen his ways, but I will heal him…” (Isaiah 57:18). He's seen it all, and the word that follows the "but" is heal. That "but" is the best word in the verse.
Punish would be the expected next word, and I get why you picked it. But verse 18 says, “I have seen his ways, but I will heal him…” The turn comes right there at the "but." God goes toward healing.

Abandon is what you'd fear after hearing verse 17, I'll give you that. But God says, “I have seen his ways, but I will heal him…” (Isaiah 57:18). He goes on to say He will guide him and restore comfort. That's the opposite of walking away.
Close, but the verse is wider than that. The LORD says, “Peace, peace to those far and near…” (Isaiah 57:19). Far AND near, both. The peace goes out in every direction.
False is right. In verse 19 the LORD says, “Peace, peace to those far and near…” and says He will heal them. He says peace twice, and He says it to the far ones too.
Be still. Verse 20 says the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea, because “…it cannot be still…” It's a washing machine stuck on spin with a lopsided load. The waves keep going and going.
Reaching the shore is a fair thought for a sea picture. But verse 20 says the sea “…cannot be still…” Its waves churn up mire and muck. The problem isn't getting anywhere, it's never settling down.

Rising higher sounds like what a storm sea does. But the verse says something else: “…it cannot be still…” The sea in this picture is restless, and its waves churn up mire and muck. Stillness is the thing it can't find.

That's a reasonable guess after all the peace in verse 19, but the passage ends differently. The last verse says there is no peace for the wicked. The same God who says peace, peace to those far and near also says that. The ending is a serious one.

False is right. Verse 21 closes the passage by saying there is no peace for the wicked. It comes right after the picture of the storm-tossed sea that cannot be still. It's a sober ending, so I'll let it sit.
